t: How To Drench Your Students In Learning
q: One of the biggest mistakes teachers make is that they get too involved in student work.
In fact, once your students become absorbed in independent or group work, once they’re doing as you ask, it’s best to observe from a distance.
When your students are on task and engaged in the work you’ve given them, it’s a sign that deep learning is taking place.
One of the goals of effective teaching is to continually extend the amount of time your students work independently and without your input.
It means that you’ll take note of their strengths, weaknesses, and struggles in order to inform future instruction.
Set your students up for success, then step off the stage . Recede into the shadows.
x: Frequent teacher involvement during independent or group work interrupts and weakens deep student learning.
Frequent teacher involvement during independent or group work interrupts and weakens deep student learning.
Frequent teacher involvement during independent or group work interrupts and weakens deep student learning.
Extending independent work time without teacher interference builds grit, perseverance, and concentration.
Stepping back doesn't mean disengaging — teachers should observe closely to inform future instruction.
The teacher's job is to model and inspire, then step off the stage and let students take ownership of learning.

t: How to Read (and Actually Enjoy) More Books this Year
q: But then I stopped keeping track of how many books I read — publicly and privately — and I don't think I'll ever go back. I can't tell you how many books I read in 2015 simply because I don't keep count.

Measuring the quantity of books that I read had no clear effect on how smart or wise or good at life or joyful I was. This isn't true for everything, but it's true for reading. When I measure how much money I make and spend, there's a clear effect on how wisely I use my money.

Since there's no detectable correlation between Number of Books Read and Degree to Which Life Has Improved, I think my mind created correlations. I got proud of reading the books; I thought of myself as smart. This is really dangerous from a whole bunch of perspectives.

I could be wrong, but I don't know of any great readers from the past who worried about this, just like I don't know of any great teachers of the past who've ask, “How do I get all the points on my evaluation rubric?” They are less interested in teacher evaluation rubrics than they are in thinking deeply and clearly about teaching itself, doing the thing better.

The degree to which we gain enjoyment, wisdom, and knowledge from our reading of books depends on how clear our purposes are. The clarity of purpose with which we read significantly affects what we get from a given reading, and if you multiply that difference by the tens of thousands of minutes you'll spend reading over the next decade or so, the difference in who you become grows exponentially.

I'm not alone in advocating for the power of purposeful reading — it's the central premise of Adler and VanDoren's 1972 classic How to Read a Book . In short, Adler and VanDoren spend a book saying this: how we read should flow from why we read .
x: Stuart argues that counting books read is a weak metric that quietly corrodes a teacher's reading life, and that clarity of purpose is what actually determines what reading yields.
Stuart distinguishes metrics that change behaviour usefully, such as money spent or miles run, from Number of Books Read, which he found had no clear effect on how wise or joyful he became.
The piece closes by trailing a follow-up on a non-freaked-out approach to reading as a teacher, with the hypothesis that clearer thinking about reading improves reading instruction too.
He then turns the legalism question into a teaching analogy, comparing it to a teacher asking how to score every point on an evaluation rubric instead of thinking hard about the craft itself.

The positive claim follows: how much enjoyment, wisdom and knowledge a reader gets depends on how clear the purpose of the reading is, compounded across tens of thousands of reading minutes over a decade.
He roots the argument in Adler and Van Doren's formula that how we read should flow from why we read, and notes that most English teachers have never read that book.

t: How To Speak So Students Listen
q: If you cut the amount of talking you do by a third, and focus only on what your students need to know, then what you say will have greater impact.
When you lower your voice, however, and speak just loud enough for students in the back of the room to hear, they instinctively lean in. They stop moving and rustling.
When you repeat the same directions over and over, you train your students not to listen to you the first time. You encourage apathy and lighten their load of responsibility.
Because your students have grown accustomed to you taking on the burden for their listening, they may very well ignore you.
They’ll begin looking at you, tracking your movements, and anticipating what you want them to do next.
They’ll become empowered to do for themselves because responsibility feels good. It’s important. It fills with pride.
x: Teachers who talk less give their words greater impact and make them easier for students to tune into.
Lowering your voice, rather than raising it, causes students to instinctively lean in and pay closer attention.
Repeating directions trains students not to listen the first time; saying it once creates urgency.
Over time, students who take ownership of listening become more engaged, attentive, and self-directed.

Over time, students begin tracking the teacher's movements, anticipating directions, and taking pride in completing tasks independently — outcomes Linsin frames as evidence that responsibility has shifted appropriately…
Linsin identifies how a teacher speaks — not just what they say — as a decisive factor in classroom listening.

t: Why Gentleness Is A Strong Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
q: There is a common misconception that you must have a big presence to be an effective leader.

21st-century students respond best to a calm, even-handed approach to classroom management. They appreciate honesty and kindness. They respect it, and thus, are quick to listen and please their teacher.
Without saying a word, a gentle presence removes classroom stress, tension, and anxiety. It soothes and alleviates excitability and distraction—which are two major causes of misbehavior.
Enforcing consequences calmly and consistently diminishes the possibility that your students will argue, complain, or lie to you about their misbehavior.
Weakness is when you lose emotional control. It’s when you lecture, berate, and admonish students instead of following your classroom management plan .
Martin Luther King Jr. was gentle. So were Rosa Parks and Abraham Lincoln. And so are the happiest and most effective teachers on Earth.
x: Linsin challenges the notion that effective classroom leadership requires a big, forceful presence, arguing instead that gentleness — not weakness — is the true hallmark of influential teachers.
Gentleness, not forcefulness, is what 21st-century students respect and respond to as classroom leadership.
A gentle presence reduces classroom stress, tension, and anxiety without a word being spoken.
Enforcing consequences calmly diminishes arguing, complaining, and pushback from students.
Gentleness is distinct from weakness; weakness is losing emotional control, while gentleness signals calm confidence.

Linsin invokes historical figures known for their calm strength — Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, and Abraham Lincoln — to reinforce that gentleness and strength are not opposites but complements.

t: A Simple Craft Your Credo Classroom Activity
q: This past week allowed me the opportunity to experiment with leading three groups of my students in a Craft Your Credo classroom activity, and I'd like to share that activity with you today. Two of the groups went quite well, and one didn't.

Anyway, the point is that this week, each day has kind of gone like this: 40-50 minutes for discussing and reading the novel, and 10-20 minutes for Something Else. Something Else is usually exam review, but the past few days Something Else has been credo crafting.
Some students complete the writing task in five minutes, and others take fifteen. The reading assignment at the end of the writing allows kids to take their time and produce their best work.

Surprise: it didn't work that well. Some students were confused (my explanation was rushed); most kids didn't have enough time (i.e., they did understand the activity, and as a result needed to put a bit of thought into it); and most of the credos were of a markedly different quality than those crafted using the three-day method described above.

Before I let you go, I want to clarify that I am not a moral or philosophical relativist. Some of the things my students write in their credos I find to be not just disagreeable, but even foolish or harmful. It's unfashionable to say so, but I think there are wise, helpful beliefs, and there are short-sighted, goal-hindering ones.

Every human being operates from a belief system about the world; too few actually know what their belief system is. In prompting my students to reflect, I am hoping to help them clarify their thinking about the things they hold true.
x: Stuart's controlled failure is the most useful part of the record, since running the same activity in twelve minutes with a new group produced confusion and superficial credos, yielding the rule that learning…

The three-day structure matters more than the prompts: ten minutes to draft, ten minutes to read a text set of real credos and revise, ten minutes to produce a final draft, with the papers returned a month later for…

The three-day structure matters more than the prompts: ten minutes to draft, ten minutes to read a text set of real credos and revise, ten minutes to produce a final draft, with the papers returned a month later for…

He is explicit about why the compressed attempt failed, citing his own rushed explanation, insufficient time, and credos of markedly lower quality, and he draws the generalisable lesson that quality learning experiences…

The closing section handles the obvious objection, with Stuart stating that he is not a moral relativist and finds some student beliefs foolish or harmful, but arguing that the purpose is clarification rather than…
His underlying claim is that everyone operates from a belief system and too few know what theirs is.

t: Two Practical Reminder Strategies for Overcoming Noise-Induced Aimlessness
q: When I look at my students and I look at myself, I see that we have something in common: we are all pretty much the opposite of Leonard. We lose sight of our single, abiding purposes and instead keep in mind only the latest short-term memories — our Twitter or Facebook streams; the book we're reading right now; the most recent show we've binge-watched or podcast we've heard.

His problem was externally initiated (he got hit in the head), internally located (his condition), and practically solved (his reminder system). Our problem is externally initiated (more choices, or noise , than ever before in human history), internally located (we form habits around our favorite sources of noise), and practically solved.

First, in line with the above quoted Simple Rules , the solutions to our noise-induced aimlessness need not be complex. Francis, in an inspired moment, wrote a less-than-200-word personal credo. Later in the passage, we learn that he cultivated the habit of regularly reflecting on that credo and whether he was living it out (or whether it needed editing).

Second, if the pope can keep in mind who he is and what his purpose is despite the pressures of his job, then we can, too. If you think the pope has an easier time remaining true to his purpose than today's American public school teacher, you're not thinking clearly.

I've heard of some folks who take their Everest statement and put it on an index card and tape it to their computer monitors. But perhaps there's a benefit in sharing it with others — in the staff lounge, or (as in my example) in the front of our classrooms. This way, it's not just the reminder that can remind us of our abiding purposes in our work — our students or our colleagues can help, too.

I heard it said recently that when we're at our best we ought to prepare for when we're at our worst. January, the month of resolutions and life-changey things , is often a month in which we're at our best. Before the month ends, schedule the time to create something — a Francis-esque credo, a Stuart-esque hand-scrawled chart paper — to remind Future You what in the world it was that you set out to do when the tougher months of February or May come along this year.
x: He argues for posting the Everest statement publicly in the classroom or staff lounge instead of taping it to a monitor, so colleagues and students share the job of reminding you.
Stuart's structural claim is that our aimlessness is externally initiated, internally located and practically solvable, which is why the fix is a physical reminder rather than more willpower.

The first practice comes from Chris Lowney's account of Pope Francis, who wrote a personal credo of under two hundred words before ordination and has revisited it for decades; Stuart asks readers to write and…
He argues for posting the Everest statement publicly in the classroom or staff lounge instead of taping it to a monitor, so colleagues and students share the job of reminding you.
He argues for posting the Everest statement publicly in the classroom or staff lounge instead of taping it to a monitor, so colleagues and students share the job of reminding you.
The timing advice is the memorable move: build the reminder during the month you are at your best so it survives the months when you are at your worst.

t: Teaching Success in a Noisy World
q: I've written before on information overload , but a recent read gave me a much better word for what I'm getting at: noise . You and I and every one of our students live in a world so unprecedentedly full of noise that we, as a species, are literally figuring out how to deal with it for the first time.

This is clarifying. The problem isn't just information — it's the choices so much information presents us with. How, then, do we teach our students (and ourselves) to manage themselves when we have next to no historically validated model for doing so?
If we're going to manage ourselves better — and help our students do the same — noise reduction is the place to start. This is, according to Drucker, perhaps the 21st century skill.

But noise reduction is way harder for some of our kids than it is for others. Ninth grader Naddyia, who shares a one bedroom apartment with five family members and has unlimited use of her smart phone, has a lot more work to do than her classmate Paris, who has her own bedroom and a mandatory “no cell phone” study time each night. You can't just tell Naddyia to “be grittier” or “do her homework” if you're going to do all in your power to promote her long-term flourishing .

When I talk to my kids about Duckworth's bedroom classroom concept, I don't expect that it will lead to drastic life changes for all of them. I do expect, though, that of my 100+ students, a percentage are going to take the idea and run. And, since I don't invest a ton of time into this — again, we're talking a 5-10 minute warm-up style activity that won't sideline my content and curricula — I'd call this a fantastic use of time.
Rather, it's that being a better and saner teacher means practicing what we teach . If we're going to teach noise reduction, we need to practice it ourselves.
x: Stuart argues that the defining problem facing both teachers and students is not information but noise, meaning the sheer volume of choices that modern life presents.
Stuart argues that the defining problem facing both teachers and students is not information but noise, meaning the sheer volume of choices that modern life presents.
The piece ties teacher credibility to teacher practice, arguing that being a saner teacher means living the noise reduction you assign to students.

The Naddyia and Paris contrast is the article's sharpest instructional point: exhortations to be grittier are useless when a student's home environment supplies the obstacle, so environment design has to be taught…
He borrows Angela Duckworth's idea that students should become the teachers of their own bedroom classrooms, and recommends a five to ten minute warm-up activity rather than a new unit.
The piece ties teacher credibility to teacher practice, arguing that being a saner teacher means living the noise reduction you assign to students.

t: An Easy Way To Keep Your Cool When Students Misbehave nts-misbehave/
q: The advice is this: When enforcing consequences, think like a referee.
A referee’s job is to make sure players abide by the agreed-upon rules of the game. That’s it. They make no judgments or decisions of their own accord.
A good referee is defined by their calm and consistent adherence to the rule book—the purpose of which is to make the game safe and fair for all participants.
Teachers who are inconsistent and enforce consequences based on how the misbehavior makes them feel, who is doing the misbehaving, or the perceived severity of the misbehavior also lose control.
As soon as a student strays from your rule book ( classroom management plan ), follow through like a referee in the Super Bowl.
Because when you focus on being a good referee, not only will you have excellent control of your class, but keeping your cool will be easy.
x: Revisiting reader-favorite advice, Linsin offers a simple mental model for staying calm while enforcing consequences: think like a referee.
A good referee follows a fixed rule book consistently, which keeps a game (or classroom) fair and under control.
A good referee follows a fixed rule book consistently, which keeps a game (or classroom) fair and under control.

Applying the analogy directly to teaching, Linsin argues that teachers who base consequences on mood, favoritism, or perceived severity — rather than on a fixed classroom management plan — similarly lose control…

t: The #1 Problem with New Years Life-Changey Stuff - Clarity of Purpose
q: Maybe you're a “ one word ” person, or a classic resolution-setter, or a jaded New Years apathist. Regardless, here's all I have to say: without clarity of purpose, resolutions, goals and words are destined to disappoint. Importantly, this principle extends way beyond efforts at personal improvement; clarity of purpose is critical with things like school improvement initiatives and literacy frameworks .

But again and again and again when I travel around the country or read reader comments, I see educators languishing for lack of clear purpose. Every year in my classes, I see students of every background and ability level frustrated by what they see as the purposelessness of high school.

When I became a teacher in 2006, my purpose was vague: I wanted to “make a positive impact on students' lives.” Several years ago, I modified that into the clearer “Mount Everest” of promoting long-term student flourishing [1]. My working life is dedicated to that single purpose: every lesson I teach and word I write and workshop I lead is aimed at promoting long-term flourishing, either for my students or for yours.

Working from this clarity of purpose, I'm less likely to, as McKeown says, “waste time and energy on the trivial many.” Put positively, clarity of purpose makes me far more likely to do the right work, the work that benefits my students and my career long term.

Instead of “it's smart for me to be up each night until the wee hours grading essays,” I can prioritize things like sleep and family . After all, modeling how one lives a flourishing (and therefore balanced) life is one way I seek to promote long-term flourishing in my students.

But I can tell you, off the top of my head, what my purpose is, and I can give you examples of how I work toward that purpose day in and day out. Ask me one hundred times, “Dave, what are you ultimately driving at?” and I'll give you the same answer each time.
x: Stuart argues that resolutions, one-word themes and goals all fail without clarity of purpose, and that the same deficiency wrecks school improvement initiatives and literacy frameworks.
He also reports seeing educators languishing for lack of clear purpose and students frustrated by what they see as the purposelessness of high school.

He then supplies his own case, tracing his purpose from the vague ambition of making a positive impact on students' lives in 2006 to the sharper formulation of promoting long-term student flourishing.

He borrows the evidence from Greg McKeown's Essentialism, which reports that clarity of purpose consistently predicts how people do their jobs and that without it people waste energy on the trivial many.
Choosing sleep and family over midnight grading is defended not as self-care but as modelling a flourishing life for students, which folds teacher workload into the purpose itself.

The test he applies to himself is memory, since goals needed a spreadsheet to recall while purpose could be stated identically a hundred times, which he offers as the practical marker of real clarity.

t: How To Ask Your Students For The Moon . . . And Get It d-get-it/
q: I’ve since learned that as long as you create a classroom your students look forward to, you can’t ask for too much. You can’t have expectations that are too high.
Your students will rise to meet your high bar as long as they know you care enough to make it worth their while.
As long as you make your classroom an experience they enjoy being part of—better yet, love being part of—they will follow you to the ends of the earth.
He never mentioned the lengthy independent work periods, the demand for flawless routines, or my neverending calls for excellence.
Because when a spirit of fun and humor are part of the fabric of your classroom, you can ask for more and for better every day of the week.
x: Students who experience a classroom as genuinely enjoyable will look back fondly on hard work and high expectations rather than resent them.
As long as students feel a class is worth their while, they will follow a teacher's high expectations willingly.
Rigorous work habits and demanding routines can coexist with — and even be remembered as part of — a beloved classroom experience.
The former student recalls the hard work, the challenging routines, and the neverending calls for excellence not as burdens but as cherished memories tied to fun, friendship, and connection.
A spirit of fun and humor in the classroom fabric enables teachers to ask more of students without pushback.

t: A Simple Back from Winter Break Classroom Activity
q: But I love the challenge of helping my students grapple with these challenges. And so even though there's a lot I want to accomplish in class during the first weeks of January, I'm going to take the time on our first day back for a simple thinking, writing, and speaking activity.

While many of my ninth grade students have at least a faint outline in their concept of “ Future Me ,” far too few consistently build goals backward from there [1]. This is partly a motivational problem — it's hard to be motivated by a vague aspiration (e.g., “I want to be a diesel mechanic because they make good money and I like trucks”) — and it's partly a skills problem — they haven't been adequately coached in goal-setting and goal-keeping (after all, those aren't on many standards lists) — and it's partly a mindset problem (e.g., “Boring things are dumb,” or “School is pointless”).

Again, I'm spending that minute walking around the class to get some formative intel on how their re-reading and revision work is going. If it turns out to be a confusing task, I re-phrase it or replace it with something else.

If you feel like 30 seconds isn't enough, try 45 or 60. The key here is that you don't want this activity to last for an entire period; I want to end class with at least a few minutes for our regular curriculum.

I'll take a handful of volunteers. Volunteer kids at this point in the year are often very comfortable speaking in front of the class; as a result, they sometimes struggle with efficient use of the floor — hence the 10 second limit.

In one month, I'll do just that. I predict that I'll find a mixed bag: some kids will have made progress, others won't. As a class, we'll spend 5-10 minutes discussing what might have caused our success or failure in keeping committed to our goals, and we'll make modifications from there.
x: Stuart lays out the lesson he uses on the first day back in January, a short thinking, writing and speaking sequence that moves students from a vague sense of their future to three written goals.

He also splits student failure to build goals backward into three causes, a motivation problem from vague aspirations, a skills problem because goal-setting is not on standards lists, and a mindset problem about school…

The time machine prompt works because it demands specificity about relationships, work and life outside work, and is immediately followed by a re-read in which students underline concrete details or add one.
Stuart lays out the lesson he uses on the first day back in January, a short thinking, writing and speaking sequence that moves students from a vague sense of their future to three written goals.

Stuart is deliberate about the timing devices, defending the thirty-second conversation limit because students struggle to sustain an externally set conversation, and the ten-second share limit because confident…

The accountability loop is what distinguishes this from a one-off new-year exercise, since students submit one goal and get it back a month later for a class discussion of what caused success or failure.
